study.sample: 493 coins in range, 31,309 readings 15 minutes apart, 2,293 sample entries (each coin's first reading in each 6-hour block)
findings: Pushes cooled off. Coins up 30-60% from their 6-hour low fell 8.2% on average over the next 4 hours (median -9.0%, 68% no higher); up 60-100%, they fell 12.1% (74% no higher). Coins within 10% of their 6-hour low were flat (+0.4%, half higher). Coins that had tripled or more were lottery tickets: most fell (median -19.8%), a few kept running.

No buy rule cleared costs. Nine entry rules, each tried with 15 exits, and 22 entry filters with a +20% target all lost money on average at $500 a trade. The least bad (coins not pushed, with $100k+ of liquidity or flat on busy volume) lost about 1.7-1.8% a trade with a +20% target sold within 8 hours.
Costs decide most of it: at $500 a side cost a median 2.2% (a 1% allowance for fees plus price impact), so a round trip needs about +4.5% just to break even; at $100 it is about 2.5%.

Selling into strength beat holding: a +10% target sold within 8 hours lost 5.4% a trade on the sample entries against 8.9% for holding 8 hours. Stops did little on their own (-8.7% with a 15% stop) and selling 15% below the peak (-7.2%) still trailed the target: at one price every 15 minutes, a stop fills after the drop.
One market: the coins in range fell 13% on average over 24 hours in this window. Rules that lost here could work in a rising market, which is why the bench keeps testing them forward.

study.sample: 7,476 sample entries on 419 coins (each coin's first reading in each hour) replayed on GeckoTerminal's 5-minute candles, in 4 walk-forward folds; 44% of the sample trades made money after costs, averaging -5.3%. Attention was not recorded yet, so the study used the market and price variables only
findings: The models found ranking signal that random scores did not: random forest ranked winners above losers with an out-of-sample AUC of 0.673, gradient boosting, XGBoost and LightGBM 0.666-0.667 and logistic regression 0.627, against 0.498 for random scores.

None of it paid after costs. Every model's top fifth of picks still lost money on average: gradient boosting -3.7% a trade and random forest -4.5%, against -5.1% for all test trades. Models of the return itself came closest: random forest on returns averaged -0.7% on 1,173 trades (t -1.1), still a loss.

Boosted trees overfit most: training AUCs of 0.89-0.97 against about 0.67 out of sample, which is why every tree model here is shallow with large leaves. k nearest neighbours memorised its training set (training AUC 1.000) and made no picks out of sample; naive Bayes, the neural network and the LSTM ranked worse (0.56-0.60).
Exit models did not beat a +10% target sold within 8 hours: following them changed the average by -0.20 to +0.18 points a trade (t under 1) on 5,989 trades.

So ranking beats chance, but the edge found so far is smaller than the 4-5% a round trip costs at $500. A model earns a live signal only if its forward picks clear those costs; on this evidence the likeliest result is that they will not, and the tab will show it either way.
